money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The local currency is the North Korean Won (KPW). Foreigners are not allowed to use the North Korean Won. Foreigners are required to use foreign currency. The Euro is the most widely accepted foreign currency. US dollars and Chinese yuan are also widely accepted. Changing currencies in North Korea is difficult. ATMs aren't available. Banking facilities are limited, and traveller's cheques aren't accepted. You can't use a debit or credit card to withdraw cash from a bank. laws.rule: Authorities have arrested and detained foreigners, including Australians. Culture and politics influence authorities when making arrests, not just the law. You may be arrested, detained or expelled for activities that aren't crimes in Australia. Authorities closely watch travellers. They may search belongings in your hotel room or monitor your email, internet, phone and fax usage.
laws.heading: Arbitrary arrest and detention

laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe. Trafficking can result in an indefinite jail sentence. Parole is rare in drug-related cases. - Carrying or using drugs
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Authorities arrest and detain people for many activities. Penalties can be very harsh. Many seemingly innocent activities may be perceived as spying. It's illegal to take photos of anything other than designated public tourist sites, including: roads and bridges airports rail stations ports government buildings scenes of poverty anything that may give a negative impression of North Korea Always ask your North Korean guide for permission before taking photos. It's illegal to: bring items that may be seen as religious, pornographic or political bring or view South Korean products or content not declare published material or electronic devices when you enter knowingly or unknowingly possess ite

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Insults or jokes about the political system or leaders are taken very seriously; visitors have been arrested for not showing enough respect, including to images of the leaders, and one was sentenced to 15 years of hard labour over a political banner. Ask your guide before taking any photograph and do not point cameras at officials or guarded buildings.

visa-preparation.entry_summary: Smartraveller advises Do not travel. A visa is needed for all travel. There is no North Korean mission in Australia, so the visa is sought in another country, such as China or Indonesia. Business travellers generally need a North Korean sponsor and Foreign Ministry permission; journalists need special permission.
visa-preparation.fastest_entry: No route published by North Korean authorities on the pages read; Smartraveller points to the DPRK Embassy in Indonesia.
visa-preparation.before_departure: Get the visa abroad, plus a double or multiple-entry China visa if travelling through China. Expect to provide recent travel itineraries, declare all published material and communications devices on arrival, and register within 24 hours (usually through the host or hotel).

steps.step: Apply for a visa outside Australia, for example through the DPRK Embassy in Indonesia.
If travelling through China, get a double or multiple-entry Chinese visa so you can re-enter China.
Declare all books, papers and communications devices on arrival; expect inspection or confiscation.
Register with the authorities within 24 hours of arrival, through the host organisation or hotel.
Check Australian sanctions on what can be taken to North Korea.

documents: Chinese double or multiple-entry visa if transiting China
open_questions: What fee and process does the DPRK Embassy in Indonesia apply to Australian applicants?
